title: DDD language and models
idea: Domain-driven design (DDD) shapes code around the business's own language, splits it into bounded contexts, and builds each model from entities and value objects.

analogy.text: In a hospital, "patient" means a bed and a chart on the ward, but an account and a bill in finance. Each department keeps its own meaning.
analogy.breaks: Departments share people; your contexts share data only through explicit translation.

points: Ubiquitous language: class and method names use the domain experts' exact words.
A bounded context is a boundary inside which each term has one meaning.
An entity has an identity that stays while its attributes change.
A value object is immutable and equal to any other with the same values.

steps.caption: In Sales, a customer is a `Buyer`: an entity with id C-7 and a credit limit.
`SalesOrder` O-1 checks its amount against the buyer's limit, in Sales words.
Shipping never asks about credit. Its model holds only what a courier needs.
The order crosses the boundary through one translator, not by sharing the `Buyer` class.
The translator builds a `Parcel` and a `Recipient` value from the sales data.
Renaming the buyer keeps entity C-7. A new address means a whole new `Recipient` value.

code.title: Value object vs entity
code.caption: `Money` is equal by value and never changes. `Customer` is equal by id, whatever its name.

walk.text: The compact constructor checks every value, so an invalid `Money` can never exist.
`plus` returns a new `Money`; neither operand changes.
Records compare by fields, so two separate 500-cent EUR values are equal.
`Customer` bases `equals` and `hashCode` on the id alone.
A renamed customer is still the same customer: identity outlives attributes.
Domain rules live in the value: mixing currencies is refused.

code.title: Two bounded contexts
code.caption: Sales and Shipping each model the same person their own way. One translator connects them.

walk.text: Sales words: a `Buyer` with a credit limit, and an order that checks it. Records keep it short.
Shipping words: a `Recipient` value and a `Parcel`. No credit, no id.
The translator is the one place that knows both models.
Each context answers its own question: credit in Sales, delivery in Shipping.

pitfalls: Do not share one huge `Customer` class across contexts; each context models its own.
Do not give value objects setters; replace the whole value instead.
Do not base an entity's `equals` on mutable fields like name; compare ids.

quiz.q: Using the classes above, what does this print?
quiz.why: `Money` is a record, so equality compares fields. `Customer.equals` compares only the id, and both ids are C-1.

takeaway: Speak the domain's language; values compare by content, entities by identity.

starters: How do I find the bounded contexts in a new system?
Should a value object ever be mutable?
